title: Receipts that are a cent off

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo prints receipts for three real orders.

tasks.title: Catch a receipt that does not add up
tasks.description:
Before you change anything, prove the bug. In `src/reproduce.js`, implement `reproduceCentDrift()`.

Pick an order and run it through the original `receipt()`. Return an object with:

- `lines` and `discountPercent`: the order you used
- `shown`: exactly what `receipt(lines, discountPercent)` returned
- `correct`: the receipt you worked out by hand for the same order, in the same `{ subtotal, discount, total }` shape with two decimal strings

The check runs your function against the original `receipt.js`. It passes when `shown` is real, `correct` is right, and the two differ.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and do the subtraction on the first receipt yourself.
Use `ticketOrder` from `orders.js` and call `receipt()` with it.
Work out the right receipt in whole cents on paper and write it as `correct`.
Run the demo again and compare `shown` with `correct`.
hints: Check the ticket receipt: does subtotal minus discount equal the total it prints?
Ten percent of 42.65 is 4.265, exactly half a cent. The team rule says half a cent rounds up.
The right ticket receipt has a discount of 4.27, and the total is subtotal minus that rounded discount.

tasks.title: Make every receipt add up
tasks.description:
Fix `receipt(lines, discountPercent)` in `src/receipt.js` so every receipt is right to the cent.

- `subtotal` is the sum of `price * qty` for every line. Prices have at most two decimals.
- `discount` is `discountPercent` of the subtotal, rounded to the nearest cent. Half a cent rounds up.
- `total` is exactly `subtotal - discount`.
- All three are strings with two decimals, like `'38.38'`. An empty order gives `'0.00'` everywhere.

The check compares your receipts with the right ones for a few hundred orders, including half cent discounts and a 100% discount.
nextSteps: Turn each price into a whole number of cents before you multiply or add.
Work out the discount in cents and round it once.
Build the total from the rounded discount, then format all three.
Run `node src/demo.js` and check each receipt adds up.
hints: The cause is not toFixed itself. It is that 18.15 and 4.265 cannot be stored exactly as binary fractions, so every step works on a value that is slightly off.
A price like 18.15 becomes a safe whole number with `Math.round(price * 100)`. Sums and products of whole numbers are exact.
Keep everything in cents until the very end, and only divide by 100 when you format. The total should be subtotal cents minus discount cents.

tasks.title: Write the test that would have caught it
tasks.description:
Write vitest tests in `src/receipt.test.js` that guard this bug for good. Assert exact receipts with `toEqual`, for orders where the cents are tricky, such as the ticket order.

The check runs your test file three times: beside the original `receipt.js` (it must fail), beside a correct fix (it must pass) and beside a fix that keeps adding floats but rounds each value with `Math.round(value * 100) / 100` at the end (it must fail).
nextSteps: Assert the full ticket receipt with `toEqual`.
Add an order where only the total is wrong, then run `npx vitest run src/receipt.test.js`.
Ask yourself which line of the receipt the rounding fix still gets wrong.
hints: Compare whole objects, not just the total. A receipt can have the right total and the wrong discount.
`Math.round(4.265 * 100)` is not 427. Try it in `node -e` and see why rounding at the end does not save you.
The ticket order catches the rounding fix on the discount line. The group order catches the original on the total line.
